content: The policy implemented in December 2006 included a 20% price reduction for off-patent pharmaceuticals, a price agreement for new chemical entities, and a positive reimbursement list. Insurance claims data were utilized to evaluate the impact on both price and volume of all recorded data. Sub-analyses were conducted specifically for antihypertensive and antihyperlipidemic medications. Although the study period spanned from 2003 to 2008, the interpretation of post-intervention data was limited to seven months due to a co-intervention introduced in August 2007. Suh et al. and Yoo et al. examined the effects of the Single Price System (SPS), which was implemented in South Korea in 2012. The latter two studies focused on specific patient subgroups and analyzed data over shorter timeframes (2009–2013 and 2011–2013, respectively), while the former study included monthly data over a decade to assess the impact on all medicines. Data for these studies were provided by the National Health Insurance (NHI), which covers 97% of the population. Suh et al. also incorporated data from Medical Aid, an insurance program covering the remaining 3% of the population, but restricted their analysis to adult beneficiaries with at least one claim for diabetes mellitus. The impact of the SPS was assessed in terms of both price and volume, with a co-intervention introduced in October 2010 prior to the SPS. Yoo et al. analyzed a random 1% sample of patients diagnosed with primary hypertension from the National Patient Sample (NPS), which included data from both the general population and low-income segments. The four Interrupted Time Series (ITS) studies reported changes in both level and trend at the time of intervention. Suh et al. and Yoo et al. also examined the impact of the SPS on monthly costs per patient. The studies calculated unit prices of all medicines from 2007 to 2016, segmented by the SPS implementation in April 2012. Antihypertensive drug costs were also segmented by the SPS, the introduction of guidelines for antihypertensive drugs in January 2013, and the Benefit Enhancement Plan in September 2013. Bergman et al. studied the impact of a 35% price reduction for off-patent originator and generic pharmaceuticals in July 2009, using pharmacy-level dispensing data from 2006 to 2011. Due to multiple co-interventions, starting in October 2009, distinguishing the specific impact of the intervention was challenging. Bergman et al. applied a regression model to estimate the effect of the price link on the logarithm of cost per defined daily dose (DDD), using costs as the dependent variable and including covariates. They reported an 87% reduction in costs per DDD. Volume-related outcomes were also reported by the four ITS studies, with some subgroups showing negligible differences. Of the 26 studies included in this systematic review, 11 assessed the impact of generic reference pricing, eight examined therapeutic reference pricing, two analyzed mixed effects of generic and therapeutic reference pricing, and five investigated the impact of generic price linkage on price and volume. No studies evaluated the effects of external reference pricing (ERP) on price and volume. Most studies employed repeated measures or interrupted time series designs. Despite heterogeneity in policies, all four sub-interventions (generic reference pricing, therapeutic reference pricing, and generic price linkage) led to price reductions, while effects on volume were less clear. Increases in volume were observed only for certain medicines, such as low-cost drugs. Generic reference pricing (GRP) reduced prices and increased the volume of generics, low-cost medicines, and parallel imports, while decreasing the volume of originator and high-cost medicines. Therapeutic reference pricing (TRP) lowered pharmaceutical expenditure, insurer costs, and medicine prices but increased patient cost-sharing. Volume effects were unclear, except for increased volume of reimbursable medicines, generics, and medicines free of cost-sharing. The impact of a mix of generic and therapeutic reference pricing on price was inconclusive, with slightly more savings in TRP and increased volume for reimbursable medicines. Studies on generic price linkage supported an association with initially lower prices, but long-term beneficial effects on prices were unlikely, and no clear association with prescription quantities was observed. The general lack of effect of the interventions was attributed to changes in utilization patterns, with a shift to pharmaceutical products not targeted by the policy. This was compounded by the absence of demand-side measures aimed at influencing prescribing behavior. The majority of studies focused on high-income countries, with limited data from Asia and no studies from Latin America or Africa. Many studies examined only one medicine group, and co-interventions occurring around the same time as the main intervention introduced potential bias. Most studies assessed price effects in terms of cost or pharmaceutical expenditure, with only two studies evaluating patient costs. The quality of evidence was judged as moderate, with methodological rigor and transparency noted in most studies. Other reviews generally agreed with these findings, highlighting that reference pricing systems, including GRP and TRP, drive down drug prices and increase the use of targeted drugs. However, therapeutic reference pricing may increase patient cost-sharing. External reference pricing (ERP) was noted to have potential drawbacks, such as launch delays and higher prices in low-income countries. Future research should focus on lowand middle-income countries, assess long-term savings, and consider the administrative burden of maintaining reference pricing systems.
